1170.title: The lifespan of the Tathagata (Kern ch. 15)
1170.hook: the Buddha reveals he awakened countless ages ago and is always present
1170.howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, this chapter is often recited, especially its verses, and some schools, including Tiantai and Nichiren traditions, treat it as the heart of the sutra.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ground split open and bodhisattvas nobody knew rose up, all taught by the Buddha himself. Your line: they rose from the earth. And Maitreya was left asking how.

A prince of the Sakya clan leaves his palace, sits under a tree near the town of Gaya, and wakes up. Not so long ago. That's what makes yesterday's crowd from under the earth impossible. Before he explains, the Buddha does something unusual. More than once he says: trust what I'm about to tell you. And more than once, the whole assembly asks him to go on. A teacher who asks for trust before speaking is about to say something hard to hear.
screen: `A PRINCE, A TREE, NEAR GAYA.` → `NOT SO LONG AGO?` → `TRUST WHAT I TELL YOU.`

segments.voice: First, the story the world believes. Gods and people all think, the Buddha says, that Shakyamuni left the Sakya palace and woke at the seat near Gaya. Second, what he actually says: it's been ages beyond reckoning since I awoke. He reaches for a picture like chapter seven's, only larger. Grind whole worlds into dust and drop a grain each time you pass a vast stretch of worlds, until the dust runs out. Then grind every world you passed, landed on or not, into dust, and let each grain be an age. More time than that has gone by since he woke, and all through it he has been here in this world, teaching. Third, why he seems to leave. If people could see him every day, the ones with little root of goodness would grow lazy, take him for granted, and stop feeling that meeting a Buddha is rare. So he appears to pass into nirvana. He calls it a skillful means, and tomorrow he tells a story about a doctor to explain it. Fourth, the verses. He is always here, he says, on the mountain called Vulture Peak, teaching. People with confused eyes don't see him, even when he's near. When people long to see him with their whole heart, he and his assembly appear. Some schools treat this chapter as the heart of the whole sutra. Its claim is simple and enormous: the Buddha hasn't left. In its words, he is always here, and people just don't always see him.
screen: `THE STORY THE WORLD BELIEVES.` · `AGES BEYOND DUST.` · `WHY HE SEEMS TO LEAVE.` · `ALWAYS HERE, ON VULTURE PEAK.` · then, large: `ALWAYS HERE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who is far from you, in another city, another country, or, if it feels right, someone no longer living. Notice what of them you still carry, a phrase they use, the way they laugh, a thing they taught you. Rest with them nearby for a few breaths, as close as the breath.
The lifespan of the Tathagata. Awake for ages beyond counting, teaching all along, seeming to pass away only so people won't take him for granted. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: always here. Not always seen, he says, but here all along. See you tomorrow.

1171.title: The physician's sons (Kern ch. 15)
1171.hook: a doctor's children take poison; he leaves word he's died so they'll take the medicine
1171.howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, the parable of the physician and his sons is told with the chapter on the Buddha's lifespan, to explain why the Buddha appears to pass away though he is always present.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha said he woke ages beyond counting ago, and only seems to leave. Your line: always here. Today, he explains why.

Nobody in the house will touch the bottle on the counter. It's the right medicine, and everybody knows it would help. Still it sits there, because it smells strange, or tastes bitter, or because taking it would mean admitting something's wrong. The Buddha promised a reason why he only seems to pass away, and he gives it the way the Lotus likes to: as a story. A doctor, a house full of children, a poison, and a medicine nobody touches.
screen: `A BOTTLE ON THE COUNTER.` → `THE RIGHT MEDICINE.` → `NOBODY TOUCHES IT.`

segments.voice: First, the poison. A wise and skilled physician has many sons. While he travels abroad, the children get into some poison and drink it. When he comes home they're writhing on the floor, and they see him and cry out: father, you're back, help us. Second, the split. He mixes a medicine that looks, smells and tastes good. Some sons, whose minds the poison hasn't reached, take it at once and are healed. The others are glad to see him and ask to be cured, but won't take it. The poison has turned their minds; the medicine seems wrong to them. Third, the message. So the father makes a plan. I'm old, he tells them, my time is near. Here's the medicine. Take it. Then he goes away again and sends a messenger home with the news that their father has died. The sons are crushed. If he were here, he'd look after us; now we're alone. And that grief brings them back to themselves. They look at the medicine, see that it's good, take it, and are healed. When the father hears, he comes home, and they see him again. Fourth, the question. Did that physician tell a lie? the Buddha asks. No, says the assembly. Neither do I, says the Buddha. I seem to pass away so that people, missing me, will turn to the teaching I've left. It's the same move as the burning house and the phantom city, and this time it's a father who wanted his children well more than he wanted them to see him.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you know is good for you that keeps sitting on the counter: a hard conversation, an apology, a night of real sleep, a call you keep not making. Notice what makes it seem bitter, without arguing with it. Then picture yourself picking it up and taking it, simply, the way the first sons did.
The physician's sons. Children who wouldn't take the cure until word came that their father was gone, and then they did. Today's word.
Your line: take the medicine. It was good all along; only the poison made it seem wrong. Go gently.

1172.title: Measure of merit (Kern ch. 16)
1172.hook: the merit of hearing that the Buddha's life is endless
1172.howItsDone: In schools that center the Lotus Sutra, such as Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren Buddhism, people read, recite and copy the sutra and speak of the merit of faith and joy in hearing it; in a range of Buddhist schools, the merit of a practice is dedicated to the good of others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the physician's sons: children who had drunk poison, and a father who sent word of his own death so they would finally take what he left them. Your line: take the medicine.

A phone lights up on the kitchen counter. Three words: the scan's clear. Nothing in the kitchen moves; the kettle is still warming. And yet the person holding the phone sits down, because the whole afternoon has changed shape. News can do that. It changes nothing you can touch and everything about the day. The chapter before this one gave its listeners news like that: the Buddha's life is beyond measure, and he is always here. Chapter sixteen, in Kern's numbering, asks what it is worth simply to hear it.
screen: `THREE WORDS ON A PHONE.` → `NOTHING MOVES, EVERYTHING CHANGES.` → `WHAT IS HEARING WORTH?`

segments.voice: First, the word. Merit, punya in Sanskrit, is the Buddhist name for the good an action sets growing, the way a seed keeps working long after it goes into the ground. You met it in year one, sharing the merit at the end of practice. Buddhists speak of making merit through giving, good conduct and meditation, and of dedicating it to the good of others. Second, the measure. The Buddha speaks to Maitreya, who, tradition says, will be the next Buddha, and sets two things side by side. On one side, someone who spends ages beyond counting practicing giving, good conduct, patience, energy and meditation. On the other, someone who hears that the Tathagata's life is this long and, for a single moment, trusts it. In the sutra's measure, the moment outweighs the ages. Third, why. One reading: the long practices are things done; the moment of trust is a thing seen. The one who hears isn't adding effort to a pile, but recognizing that what they hoped for is already here. The chapter goes further. Those who hear and keep this teaching have no need to build stupas or monasteries for him; keeping it is already that offering. And the place where someone keeps, reads or copies it is to be honored as if the Buddha stood there. Fourth, what this does to merit. Here it is not a scoreboard. Effort is not wasted, but the door opens by a moment of trust, not by the number of hours. Glad news, taken in and trusted, is already practice.
screen: `MERIT: GOOD THAT GROWS.` · `ONE GLAD MOMENT, AGES OF EFFORT.` · `KEEPING IT IS THE OFFERING.` · `NOT A SCOREBOARD.` · then, large: `GLAD NEWS.`

segments.voice: Look back through the last few days for one good thing; small is fine, a friend's message, a plant that bloomed, someone else's good fortune. Hold it without analyzing it or planning what to do with it, and if gladness comes, let it take up the whole breath. If the mind slides toward a worry, come back to the news.
Measure of merit. In the Lotus Sutra, the teaching that one moment of trust outweighs ages of effort. Today's word.
Your line: glad news. A single moment can outweigh the ages. That's today, done.

1173.title: The fiftieth listener (Kern ch. 17)
1173.hook: even the fiftieth person to hear it passed on, rejoicing, has great merit
1173.howItsDone: In schools that honor the Lotus Sutra, people rejoice in hearing it, invite others to listen, and pass its teaching on; the chapter's picture of a chain of glad hearers is read as encouragement to share the teaching, however secondhand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the measure of merit: one moment of trust, weighed above ages of effort. Your line: glad news.

A recipe card sits in a kitchen drawer, butter-stained at one corner, in an aunt's handwriting. She copied it from a neighbor, who copied it from someone nobody in the family ever met. Nobody in that chain was a chef. Each simply liked it enough to hand it on, and somewhere along the way a pinch of something got added. Chapter seventeen of the Lotus Sutra, in Kern's numbering, follows a chain like that, link by link, then asks a surprising question about the person at the very end.
screen: `A STAINED RECIPE CARD.` → `COPIED, AND COPIED AGAIN.` → `WHO IS AT THE END?`

segments.voice: First, the question. Maitreya asks what merit comes to someone who hears this teaching and rejoices in it. The Sanskrit word is anumodana: rejoicing, being glad along with someone. Not doing anything yet. Just being glad. Second, the chain. Someone hears the teaching in an assembly, goes off to a village or town, and tells it as well as they can remember to a friend or relative. That person is glad, and tells another, who tells another, on and on, until it reaches a fiftieth person, who hears it at the far end of all that retelling, perhaps a little blurred, and rejoices too. Third, the comparison. Beside that fiftieth listener stands a great patron who gives countless beings everything they could want for many years, then teaches them until they reach the highest fruits of the path. That patron's merit is enormous. And yet, the Buddha says, the fiftieth listener's gladness is greater, beyond counting. And if that is true of the fiftieth, how much more of the first. Fourth, the small acts. The chapter goes on, almost tenderly: someone who goes to hear the teaching for a little while, someone who says to a friend, come and listen with me, someone who moves over and offers part of their seat to a newcomer. Each is honored. The teaching doesn't wear thin as it travels hand to hand. The gladness travels with it, and arrives whole.
screen: `MAITREYA ASKS ABOUT REJOICING.` · `A CHAIN OF FIFTY HEARERS.` · `GLADNESS OUTWEIGHS A GREAT GIFT.` · `EVEN SHARING A SEAT.` · then, large: `PASSED ON AND ON.`

segments.voice: Name, quietly, one good thing that reached you through someone else, a book, a kindness, a way of making tea, and trace it back a link or two if you can. Then picture one person you could hand it to, and see them receiving it. Rest there, with the chain one link longer.
The fiftieth listener. In the Lotus Sutra, the one at the end of a long chain of telling, whose simple gladness still carries great merit. Today's word.
Your line: passed on and on. Gladness doesn't wear thin on the way. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1174.title: The preacher's senses (Kern ch. 18)
1174.hook: those who keep the sutra have their senses purified
1174.howItsDone: In schools that center the Lotus Sutra, keeping the sutra means reading, reciting, explaining and copying it, practices open to lay people as well as monks and nuns; this chapter describes the purified senses said to follow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fiftieth listener, still glad at the far end of a long chain of telling. Your line: passed on and on.

Turn off the music, close the laptop, and the room turns out to be full of sound: the fridge's hum, a car two streets over, a bird, a pipe ticking, your own breath. None of it is new. It was there the whole time, underneath. Chapter eighteen of the Lotus Sutra, in Kern's numbering, is about senses made clear like that. It promises the one who keeps this teaching eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body and mind that take in the world without fog.
screen: `MUSIC OFF, ROOM FULL OF SOUND.` → `IT WAS THERE ALL ALONG.` → `SENSES MADE CLEAR.`

segments.voice: First, who the preacher is. The Sanskrit is dharmabhanaka, one who speaks the dharma. In the Lotus it isn't only a monk on a platform: it's any son or daughter of good family who keeps this teaching, reads it, recites it, explains it or copies it out. A parent reading at bedtime would count. Second, the eyes. With the very eyes their parents gave them, the Buddha says, such a person will see the whole universe, from the lowest hell to the highest heaven, and the beings in it, and how their deeds bear fruit. Not new eyes, not a third eye. The same eyes, cleared. Third, the ears. The chapter's list of what they will hear goes on and on: elephants and horses, chariots, weeping and laughter, conches, bells and drums, the voices of men, women, boys and girls, the sounds of gods and of beings in pain. And the ear takes all of it in without being overwhelmed. Fourth, body and mind. The chapter goes on through smell, taste and touch, and says the body becomes so clear that beings see themselves reflected in it, like a mirror. The mind, hearing even a single verse, finds many meanings opening from it. One way to hear all this: purified senses are not superpowers. They are senses that receive the world as it is, before the story about it takes over.

segments.voice: With eyes closed or resting low, open the ears: find the farthest sound, then the nearest, then everything in between, letting each arrive and leave without naming it. If a sound is unpleasant, notice the urge to push it away, and hear it anyway, simply as sound. If you lose the thread, the next sound will bring you back.
The preacher's senses. In the Lotus Sutra, the eyes, ears and mind of one who keeps the teaching, made clear enough to take in the world without being overwhelmed. Today's word.
Your line: clear senses. The same eyes and ears your parents gave you, only clearer. See you tomorrow.

1175.title: Never Disparaging (Kern ch. 19)
1175.hook: a bodhisattva bows to everyone: I don't despise you, you will become a Buddha; they throw stones, he bows from further off
1175.howItsDone: In Tendai and Nichiren Buddhism, Never Disparaging is held up as a model for practice in hard times, and some practitioners bow to others as a reminder that everyone can become a Buddha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the preacher's senses: the same eyes and ears, made clear. Your line: clear senses.

A monk walks up to a stranger on the road, bows low, and says: I don't despise you. You will become a Buddha. The stranger stares, then gets angry. Who asked for this man's opinion? Up comes a stick, or a handful of stones. The monk steps back out of range and says it again, louder, from further off. That is very nearly the whole of chapter nineteen in Kern's numbering, and the chapter says it went on like that for a long time.
screen: `A BOW ON THE ROAD.` → `A HANDFUL OF STONES.` → `SAID AGAIN, FROM FURTHER OFF.`

segments.voice: First, the monk. The Buddha tells of a time long ago, after an ancient Buddha had passed away, when arrogant monks held sway. A bodhisattva monk did not spend his days reciting scriptures. Whenever he saw anyone, monk or nun, layman or laywoman, he went up, bowed, and said: I do not despise you. You are walking the bodhisattva path, and you will become Buddhas. Second, why it angered people. Some heard an insult wrapped in a compliment. Who was he to make predictions about them? They shouted at him and struck at him with sticks and clods of earth. Third, what he did. He stepped out of reach and called the same words back from a distance. He didn't change his line, and he didn't strike back. That is how he got his name. In the Chinese translation it is Never Disparaging. Some readers hear two things at once in the Sanskrit name, Sadaparibhuta: the one who never despised, and the one who was always despised. Fourth, who he turned out to be. Near the end of his life, the chapter says, he heard the Lotus Sutra, his senses were made clear, just as yesterday described, and his life was lengthened so he could teach it. Those who had mocked him came to listen. Then the Buddha tells the assembly: that monk was me. And some of the people who once threw the stones are sitting here now.
screen: `A MONK WHO ONLY BOWS.` · `HEARD AS AN INSULT.` · `HE STEPS BACK AND SAYS IT AGAIN.` · `THAT MONK WAS ME.` · then, large: `I DO NOT DESPISE YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind, one at a time, people you're likely to see today, someone at home, someone at work, a stranger behind a counter, and for each let there be a small inward bow, as if to say: I see you. Then bring to mind one person who is hard for you, and offer the same small bow, from as far off as you need.
Never Disparaging. In the Lotus Sutra, the monk who bowed to everyone and told them they would become Buddhas, and who, the Buddha says, was himself in a past life. Today's word.
Your line: I do not despise you. He never once changed his line. Until tomorrow.

A notary's stamp. A handshake in front of witnesses. A signature on the line. People have many ways of saying: this counts, and I stand behind it. Chapter twenty of the Lotus Sutra, in Kern's numbering, has one of its own. The Buddhas put out their tongues. It sounds almost comic at first, and it is meant to be enormous. It's also the last day of this week, so after the scene, the week's lines get gathered up.

segments.voice: First, the scene. The bodhisattvas who rose from the cracks of the earth have just vowed to carry the teaching after the Buddha is gone. Then Shakyamuni, the ancient Buddha Prabhutaratna seated beside him in the jeweled stupa, and all the Buddhas gathered from other worlds, each on a lion seat, put out their tongues. The tongues reach up to the Brahma heaven, and rays of light pour from them. Tradition says a long, broad tongue is one of a Buddha's bodily marks, the sign of a speaker who does not lie. So the gesture isn't rude. It means: what was said here is true. Second, the sound. Then the Buddhas clear their throats and snap their fingers, all together, and the sound reaches worlds in every direction. Beings everywhere look up, see the great assembly, and are glad. Third, the handing over. With the teaching confirmed, the Buddha entrusts it to the bodhisattvas. Wherever it is kept, read or explained, in a park or a forest, under a tree, in a monastery or a family's house, that spot is to be honored as the place where Buddhas awaken. Fourth, the week, confirmed. Look back at the lines you've carried: always here, take the medicine, glad news, passed on and on, clear senses, I do not despise you. Each came from a chapter of this sutra, and today the sutra puts its own stamp on the whole book, with a gesture as wide as the worlds.
